title: Is this what I feared?
hook: Seneca: set aside days to live on very little and ask if this is what you dreaded (Letters 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday: plain food, Musonius's training. Your line was plain is training. What did you miss, and what didn't you? Day three hundred.

Day three hundred. Worth a breath of its own. Now a quieter question, one that can sit in the back of a mind for years: what if it all went away? The job, the savings, the comfortable apartment. What if I ended up with almost nothing? A fear like that can go unexamined, humming, shaping choices. Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius in the middle of a noisy Roman holiday, suggested an experiment. Not thinking about the fear. Trying it, on purpose, for a few days. Today: is this what I feared?
screen: `DAY THREE HUNDRED.` → `WHAT IF IT ALL WENT AWAY?` → `TRY IT ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: It's December in Rome, the festival of Saturnalia. The whole city is feasting, and Seneca writes that Rome is sweating with it. In the middle of this he writes his eighteenth letter. His advice: set aside a certain number of days, and live on the scantiest, cheapest food, in rough, coarse clothing. And while you do, ask yourself one question. In Richard Gummere's translation of 1917: "Is this the condition that I feared?" He gives the reason with a picture everyone in Rome would know. Soldiers practice maneuvers in peacetime, digging trenches with no enemy in sight, so that they won't panic when the real day comes. The soul should do the same in good times: train, while fortune is kind, for the day fortune isn't. And he's clear it shouldn't be a show, like rich Romans who played at poverty in fancy little rooms. Make the bed really hard and the bread really coarse. Here's a lovely detail. In the same letter Seneca quotes Epicurus, the founder of a rival school, who kept certain days of eating very little to see whether he was missing any real pleasure. Seneca borrows good ideas from wherever he finds them, and says so. Seneca's bet is that the trial teaches something. The thing dreaded turns out to be survivable, even ordinary. Plain bread is still bread. A cold room is still a room. And a fear looked at in daylight has less room to hum. The point isn't to lose everything. It's to find out, ahead of time, what you'd still have.
screen: `SATURNALIA: ROME IS FEASTING.` · `LIVE ON VERY LITTLE FOR A FEW DAYS.` · `SOLDIERS DRILL IN PEACETIME.` · `SENECA QUOTES EPICURUS.` · then, large: `IS THIS WHAT I FEARED?`

segments.voice: Pick one comfort you'll go without today. Something small but real: the second coffee, the phone at lunch, the car for a short trip, the soft chair. Now, sitting here, imagine the moment you miss it. Let the little pang come. Then ask Seneca's question gently: is this what I feared? Stay with whatever answer comes. The bell holds the time.
Saturnalia, the Roman December feast when Seneca urged practicing poverty on purpose, so fear loses its grip in good times. Today's word.
Your line: plain bread is still bread. Go without one comfort today, and when you miss it, remember the question Seneca asked. Day three hundred.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners set aside occasional days of voluntary discomfort, like simple food or skipping a convenience, to see that what they fear losing is survivable.
